body.p: Applicant submits this Reply in response to the Office Action mailed September 2, 2021.
I. Status of the Claims
By this Reply, Applicant amends claims 1, 9, and 17. The originally filed
specification and drawings fully support the subject matter of the amended and new claims. Claims 1-20 are pending in this application. Claims 1, 9, and 17 are the sole independent claims.
II. Section 103 Rejections

In the Office Action, claims 1-7, 9-15, and 17-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Taylor (US 2012/0041318) in view of Walker (Walker, T Gregory. "Mesenteric vasculature and collateral pathways" Seminars in interventional radiology vol. 26, 3 (2009): 167-74) and Phillips (US 2005/0187469). (Office Action at pages 3-13.) Claims 8 and 16 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Taylor in view of Walker and Phillips (US 2005/0187469), and further in view of Cleveland Clinic (Cleveland Clinic "Intestinal Ischemic Syndrome", https://my.clevelandclinic.org/services/heart/disorders/arterial-disease/intestinal- ischemic-syndrome). (Office Action at pages 14-15.) The rejections are respectfully traversed.
Claim 1 is amended herein to recite:
determining a threshold blood flow characteristic based on
the patient-specific anatomic model of the patient's
bowel and a predetermined healthy or average blood
flow characteristic based on a population-based
measurement or estimate

(Emphasis added.) In rejecting claim 1, the Office Action acknowledged that Taylor "does not explicitly teach 'the threshold blood flow characteristic further comprising a predetermined healthy or average blood flow characteristic based on a population-based measurement or estimate,"' as previously recited by claim 1. (Office Action at pages 9-10.) Instead, the Office Action asserted that the entirety of Phillips, but particularly claims 8 and 9, discloses such features because:
... the Examiner finds the broadest reasonable
interpretation of Phillips model index includes a threshold in
a population-based measurement or estimate. In addition,
while neither Applicant's Specification nor the cited prior art teaches the ipsa verba of the claim limitation, the Examiner
finds that even without the teaching of Phillips, that since Taylor teaches the simulated perfusion data (i.e., the
threshold blood flow characteristic) below a
predetermine threshold, the predetermined threshold is
inherently related to population-based measurement or
estimate data so that the threshold blood flow characteristic
has diagnostic and/or therapeutic efficacy.
(Office Action at page 10.) Applicant respectfully disagrees for the following reasons.

First, the Office Action relies on a "broadest reasonable interpretation" (BRI) of the disclosures of Phillips. This is an incorrect application of BRI. BRI applies to the claims under examination (MPEP 2111) not the cited references; whereas, the interpretation of a reference's disclosures is limited to that which is expressly, implicitly, or inherently disclosed. (MPEP 2112.) The disclosures of Phillips with respect to these features of claim 1 are not to be construed according to the BRI standard.

With respect to express disclosures, Phillips is directed to "measuring physiologic tissues perfusion information." (Abstract.) Claims 8 and 9 of Phillips, which were specifically cited by the Office Action, recite:
8. A method of creating a tissue perfusion index for healthy population including: (a) obtaining a measurement of blood
flow and a measurement of blood oxygen content from a
healthy patient; (b) combining said measurements to
calculate a parameter indicative of tissue perfusion in said
healthy patient; (c) repeating steps (a) and (b) on a plurality
of healthy patients to obtain a set of calculations of said
parameter for said plurality of patients; (d) processing the set
of calculated parameters to obtain a statistically averaged
index of said parameter for a healthy population.
9. A method of creating a tissue perfusion index for a
population with a known condition including: (a) obtaining a
measurement of blood flow and a measurement of blood
oxygen content from a patient with said known condition; (b)
combining said measurements to calculate a parameter
indicative of tissue perfusion in said patient; (c) repeating steps (a) and (b) on a plurality of patients with said known
condition to obtain a set of calculations of said parameter for said plurality of patients; (d) processing the set of calculated
parameters to obtain a statistically averaged index of said
parameter for a population with said known condition.
Here, Phillips at most discloses "creating a tissue perfusion index" but does not
disclose or suggest that such a "tissue perfusion index" can or should be used to
"[determine] a threshold blood flow characteristic" in conjunction with a "patient-specific
anatomic model," as recited by amended claim 1. Accordingly, the combination of
Phillips would not produce the recited features of claim 1.
With respect to implicit disclosures in Phillips, MPEP 2144.01 states: "[I]n
considering the disclosure of a reference, it is proper to take into account not only
specific teachings of the reference but also the inferences which one skilled in the art
would reasonably be expected to draw therefrom." (Quoting In re Preda, 401 F.2d 825,
826, 159 USPQ 342, 344 (CCPA 1968), emphasis added.) Applicant notes that the
example judicial decisions cited in MPEP 2144.01 each rely on disclosures in the cited
reference that lead to the asserted inference ("the reference recognized the possibility

of using temperatures greater than 750°C" in Preda, and a suggestion of a substitution of a chemical group from a limited number of possibilities in In re Lamberti, 545 F.2d 747, 750, 192 USPQ 278, 280 (CCPA 1976)).

Here, nothing cited or found in Phillips suggests that the created "tissue perfusion index" can or should be used to "[determine] a threshold blood flow characteristic" in conjunction with a "patient-specific anatomic model," as recited by amended claim 1. Thus, absent impermissible hindsight reasoning, it is not proper to conclude that one skilled in the art would reasonably be expected to read these features of amended claim
1 from the disclosures of Phillips. Accordingly, the Office Action does not make out a prima facie case that any implicit teachings of Phillips disclose these features of amended claim 1.

With respect to inherent disclosures, MPEP 2112 states: "In relying upon the theory of inherency, the examiner must provide a basis in fact and/or technical reasoning to reasonably support the determination that the allegedly inherent characteristic necessarily flows from the teachings of the applied prior art." (Quoting Ex parte Levy, 17 USPQ 2d 1461, 1464 (Bd. Pat. App. & Inter. 1990), emphasis in original.) Here, the Office Action does not provide any reasoning to show that the mere creation of a "tissue perfusion index," as disclosed by Phillips, necessarily leads to a "[determination of] a threshold blood flow characteristic" in conjunction with a "patient- specific anatomic model," as recited by amended claim 1. Accordingly, the Office Action fails to make out a prima facie case that these features of amended claim 1 are inherently disclosed by the teachings of Phillips.

Accordingly, Philli s does not disclose these features of claim 1. The remaining cited references fail to compensate for the noted deficiencies of Phillips and therefore, claim 1 is patentably distinguishable over the cited references for at least these reasons.

The above comments are specifically directed to independent claim 1. However, it is respectfully submitted that the comments would be helpful in understanding various differences of the other independent claims over the cited references. Therefore, it is

respectfully submitted that all the independent claims are patentable over the cited references. Moreover, it is respectfully submitted that the various dependent claims arepatentable over the cited references for at least the reason that they depend from anindependent claim that is patentable over the cited references.
In view of the above, it is respectfully submitted that the rejection is overcome. III. Conclusion

The Office Action contains characterization of the claims and the related art with which the Applicant does not necessarily agree. Unless expressly noted otherwise, Applicant declines to subscribe to any statement or characterization in the Office Action.
In discussing the specification, claims, and drawings in this Reply, it is to be

understood that Applicant is in no way intending to limit the scope of the claims to any exemplary embodiments described in the specification or abstract and/or shown in the drawings. Rather, Applicant is entitled to have the claims interpreted broadly to the maximum extent permitted by statute, regulation, and applicable case law.
In view of the foregoing remarks, Applicant submits that this claimed invention is neither anticipated nor rendered obvious in view of the prior art references cited against
this application. Applicant therefore requests the reconsideration and reexamination of the application, and the timely allowance of the pending claims.
